title: Abusing Men’s Bodies and Minds for Our Viewing Pleasure
author: Peter Gray
summary: Gray, a developmental psychologist, argues that American football is real rather than pretend violence and that its harm to boys and men is no longer in doubt. He walks through the evidence on chronic traumatic encephalopathy, including the finding of CTE in 110 of 111 donated NFL brains and an October 2026 JAMA study estimating about 75% of all former NFL players had CTE at death. He stresses that there appears to be no safe dose and that children as young as five or six still play adult-run tackle football. He compares the football industry's 'safer game' gestures to filters on cigarettes and the owners' behavior to tobacco denial. His proposal is a cigarette-style warning in locker rooms and on broadcasts, with parents required to sign it for young children. This is an updated version of an essay first posted three years earlier.
points: Gray frames football as real violence, unlike the pretend violence of play he defends elsewhere, which is why he treats its harms differently.
A JAMA study of 2,362 former NFL players estimated roughly 75% had CTE by death, with rates highest for those who played the most games and in the hardest-hitting positions.
There appears to be no completely safe dose of football, and CTE has been found in people who played only youth or high school football.
He likens franchise owners and universities to tobacco companies, with 'making the game safer' as the analogue of cigarette filters.
His modest policy proposal is a surgeon-general-style warning label, with parents signing for children too young to weigh it.
quotes: The data are clear. Football, which by design involves repetitive blows to the head, causes brain injury. Research has shown repeatedly that former NFL players are far more likely than others to suffer later in life from such brain disorders as Parkinson’s Disease, ALS (Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), and, especially, CTE (chronic traumatic encephalopathy.

Such damage derives not just from major crashes to the head but also from repeated smaller hits, which seem innocuous in their immediate observable effects These can be hits well below the level that results in noticeable concussions. CTE can occur in athletes in all sports that involve frequent blows to the head, but at least in modern times they are most common in football.
Using this evidence, and statistical means to correct for bias, they estimated that approximately 75% of all former NFL players had CTE by the time of their death.

Research has even revealed CTE in some who only played in youth or high school football, and some neurologists suspect that young brains may be even more susceptible to damage than more mature brains. Yet, even now, tens of thousands of children as young as 5 or 6 years old play adult-run tackle football

The case with football and CTE is like that, decades ago, with smoking and cancer. The billionaire franchise owners, and the universities enriching their coffers from it, put their heads in the sand or go through motions of “making the game safer” (analogous to putting filters on cigarettes), while doing whatever they can to obscure the science that proves the dangers and to resist any pressure to abolish or seriously change the game. Those who enjoy the product from the safety of their living room couches likewise put their heads in the sand, preferring not to see or believe the data.
I won’t watch football and I try to encourage others not to watch it. If nobody watched it, it would go away. But that’s not going to happen anytime soon.

What about children too young to understand and weigh the warning? They should be running around playing in their own joyful ways, as children are designed by nature to play, never lined up by coaches to crash into one another on command. That change would happen quickly if parents had to sign the warning.
